scenes.tts: Along the Chesapeake Bay, an osprey carries a menhaden home to its chicks. Menhaden filter tiny plankton out of the water. Phytoplankton, the plankton that photosynthesize, caught the energy first, from sunlight. So where does the osprey's energy come from? And why does there seem to be less of it at each step of a food chain?
scenes.visual: Sun, bay water bar, plankton, menhaden, osprey blocks appear one by one; question marks over the gaps
scenes.narration: Along the Chesapeake Bay, an osprey carries a menhaden home to its chicks. Menhaden filter tiny plankton out of the water. Phytoplankton, the plankton that photosynthesize, caught the energy first, from sunlight. So where does the osprey's energy come from? And why does there seem to be less of it at each step of a food chain?

scenes.tts: A producer captures energy from sunlight and stores it in food. In the open water of the Bay, the main producers are phytoplankton. A consumer gets energy by eating other living things. Zooplankton eat phytoplankton. Menhaden eat both. The osprey eats menhaden. Each feeding step is a trophic level. Arrows usually point from the food to the eater.
scenes.visual: Food chain builds left to right with level labels and arrows from food to eater
scenes.narration: A producer captures energy from sunlight and stores it in food. In the open water of the Bay, the main producers are phytoplankton. A consumer gets energy by eating other living things. Zooplankton eat phytoplankton. Menhaden eat both. The osprey eats menhaden. Each feeding step is a trophic level. Arrows usually point from the food to the eater.

scenes.tts: When a zooplankton eats a phytoplankton cell, most of that energy does not become new zooplankton. Some is released as heat during cellular respiration. Some is in parts that are not eaten or not digested. Much of that ends up with decomposers, which get energy from dead matter. Only the rest becomes new body tissue.
scenes.visual: One bar for the energy in the eaten cell splits into heat, uneaten or undigested matter, and new tissue; decomposer chip catches the uneaten part
scenes.narration: When a zooplankton eats a phytoplankton cell, most of that energy does not become new zooplankton. Some is released as heat during cellular respiration. Some is in parts that are not eaten or not digested. Much of that ends up with decomposers, which get energy from dead matter. Only the rest becomes new body tissue.

scenes.tts: As a rule of thumb, about 10 percent of the energy at one level ends up in the next. Here is a model patch of bay, with made up numbers. Phytoplankton add 100,000 kilojoules per square meter per year. Zooplankton get 10,000. Menhaden get 1,000. The osprey level gets 100. Real measurements are often higher or lower. A 2026 synthesis found an average of about 6 percent.

scenes.tts: Energy is never made or destroyed. It changes form. Light becomes chemical energy in food. Food energy becomes motion and heat. No living thing can capture that heat to build food again. So energy flows one way, in as sunlight and out as heat. Matter behaves differently. Decomposers release much of the carbon from a dead menhaden as carbon dioxide, and phytoplankton can take it up again.

Decomposers release much of the carbon from a dead menhaden as CO2, and phytoplankton can take it up again.

scenes.tts: So where does the osprey's energy come from? It began as sunlight caught by phytoplankton. At every step, much of the energy is released as heat or left in uneaten or undigested matter. So only a small share, often around 10 percent, passes upward. Much of the carbon can cycle back to the plankton, but the energy will not.
